text: bone marrow transplantation.2 A retrospective cohort study15 that compared patients older than 50 years with younger patients found that more older patients had received ciclosporin alone, that the response to immunosuppression was independent of age at the time of treatment, and that although survival decreased with age deaths were similar to those in a general population and were not related to the type of treatment or the number of courses of treatment. The outcome of pregnancy in women who had previously been treated for aplastic anaemia with an immunosuppres- sant regimen has been described.16 Of 36 pregnancies, 22 were uncomplicated and 7 were complicated by relapse of aplastic anaemia; complications appeared to be more like- ly in women with low platelet counts and paroxysmal noc- turnal haemoglobinuria. Rarely, aplastic anaemia can de- velop during pregnancy, and although the disease may remit spontaneously after termination or delivery, this does not occur in all cases.17,18 Supportive care is the mainstay for management of aplastic anaemia during pregnancy, al- though the use of ciclosporin may be considered if transfu- sions are required.2 Patients with non-severe aplastic anaemia may require supportive therapy only. For those who do require immu- nosuppression there is less evidence on which to base treatment, but one prospective study19 of patients with non-severe disease who had become transfusion-depend- ent reported that the combination of antilymphocyte im- munoglobulin and ciclosporin produced a higher response rate with an earlier onset than ciclosporin alone. Although survival was no different between the groups, combination therapy was associated with less disease progression and a higher probability of disease-free survival. 1. Young NS.
